opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot. A big part of why Transformers work so well is that most of the data we feed them has already been heavily processed. Take language: we run text through a tokenizer, and those tokens are dense with meaning. Each one is a fairly semantically rich unit, so attention, which compares every token against every other token, makes a lot of sense. You're relating meaningful chunks to each other, and attention is very good at that.

As you move toward rawer data, that stops being true. Think of characters or bytes instead of tokens, or raw audio waveforms, or genomics, or high-resolution signals from sensors. Any single element carries very little information. One audio sample at sixteen kilohertz means almost nothing by itself. Meaning only appears when you aggregate over many elements. So the sequences get much longer, and the inductive bias of attention fits less well, because pairwise interactions between tiny meaningless units aren't the right primitive.

State space models like Mamba fit naturally there. The recurrent view means you keep a compressed state that you update as the data streams in. That's essentially what you want for raw signals: you continuously absorb and summarize information instead of caching every element and looking back at all of it. You also get linear scaling in sequence length, which matters a lot when your sequences are hundreds of thousands or millions of elements long. Quadratic attention becomes prohibitive there.

We saw this empirically too. On things like audio and DNA modeling, Mamba's advantage over Transformers tended to grow as the context got longer and as the data got less processed. On heavily tokenized language the gap is smaller, and that makes sense, since that's the regime where Transformers are strongest.

More broadly, I think tokenization is something of a crutch. It's a hand-engineered preprocessing step that exists partly because attention is expensive and works best on meaningful units. It has known problems: brittleness, odd behavior on numbers and spelling, poor fit for many languages and modalities. The long-term goal I find exciting is models that learn their own abstractions directly from raw data, end to end. Architectures that handle long, low-information-density sequences efficiently, like SSMs, or hybrids that combine them with some attention, seem like the right building blocks for that. So less-processed data isn't just a niche where Mamba happens to do well. I think it points to where the field should be heading.

r001.rationale: The response says Mamba’s advantage tends to grow on less processed data, but does not state that this holds with compute matched.

r002.rationale: It explains that attention over tiny, low-information units is a poor fit and contrasts this with caching every element and looking back over all of them.

r003.rationale: It says Mamba maintains and updates a compressed state, continuously absorbing and summarizing raw signals.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think it gets at a pretty fundamental difference between how these two model classes handle information.

The way I think about it is that Transformers are really good at operating on data that's already been compressed into meaningful units. Language is the canonical example. When you tokenize text, every token carries a lot of semantic content. A word or a subword is a pretty dense, discrete piece of information. And attention is built for that regime. It looks at every token, it can retrieve any one of them exactly, and that works great when each element of the sequence is worth looking at individually.

But a lot of real-world data isn't like that. Raw audio waveforms, DNA sequences, pixels, time series from sensors, video frames. These are much closer to the raw signal. Any individual sample is pretty uninformative on its own. The information is spread out and redundant across many positions, and the meaning only emerges once you aggregate over longer contexts.

And in that setting, attention has two problems. One is just the obvious computational one. These sequences are long, often orders of magnitude longer than text, and quadratic scaling really hurts. But the more interesting problem to me is about inductive bias. Attention doesn't naturally compress anything. It wants to keep everything around and look back at it all. When most of your inputs are noisy, redundant samples, that's kind of the wrong thing to want. You're spending all your capacity attending over stuff that doesn't individually matter.

State space models, and Mamba in particular, do the opposite. They're forced to compress the history into a fixed-size state as they go. That's a constraint, and for language it was historically a weakness, which is a lot of what the selection mechanism in Mamba was trying to fix. But for raw, less-processed data, that compression is actually the right bias. The model has to learn to summarize the signal, to pull out the slowly varying structure and throw away the noise. That's essentially what you want a feature extractor to do, and it maps really nicely onto the kind of continuous-time, signal-processing roots that these models came from.

So the way I'd put it is, Transformers have kind of relied on tokenization to do a lot of the work for them. Someone has already done the hard job of turning the world into discrete, meaningful chunks. If you take that away and hand the model something closer to the raw signal, I think models that have compression built in have a real structural advantage. And honestly, that's also where I think there's the most upside, because there's so much data out there that we haven't been able to tokenize cleanly, and we've mostly just been avoiding it.

r001.rationale: The response argues that models with built-in compression have a structural advantage on raw data, but does not say that less optimized tokenizers improve alternatives’ performance relative to Transformers when compute is matched.

r002.rationale: It says attention keeps and looks back at everything, which is wasteful when inputs are noisy, redundant samples that carry little information individually.

r003.rationale: It explains that state space models, including Mamba, compress history into a fixed-size state and that this built-in compression suits raw, less processed data.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that the sequence you give a model is already the result of a lot of design choices. With language, for example, we tokenize the text, so each step is a fairly meaningful unit. If you move toward raw audio or pixels, the sequences get much longer, and each individual step might carry much less information.

That makes it an interesting setting for models like Mamba for two reasons. One is computational: you want to process those long sequences without paying the quadratic cost of attention. The other is about how you use information. You probably don’t need to retain every individual sample and compare it with every other sample. You want to absorb what’s relevant into a state and move on. Mamba’s selection mechanism gives it a way to decide, based on the input, what to keep and what to forget.

So the opportunity is to push more of that processing into the model itself, rather than relying on a preprocessing pipeline to turn the data into a short sequence first. That doesn’t automatically mean these models will be better, but I think it’s a particularly promising place to explore their strengths.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long sequences and attention’s quadratic cost, but does not say that less optimized tokenizers improve alternative models’ performance relative to Transformers at matched compute.

r002.rationale: It says each raw input step may carry little information and that a model need not retain every sample and compare it with every other one, communicating why that would be wasteful.

r003.rationale: It describes absorbing relevant information into a state and moving on, and moving more processing into the model, which communicates internal compression.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to sequence length and how much structure is already built into the representation. With language, we’ve done quite a bit of processing before the model ever sees the data. We turn text into tokens, and those tokens are already fairly information-dense. If you look at something like audio, you might have tens of thousands of samples per second. So you’re asking the model to deal with much longer sequences, where any individual sample might not tell you very much.

That’s a setting where the scaling of attention becomes a real constraint. You’d like to process the data at its original resolution and let the model learn what information to preserve, rather than having to make all those decisions in a preprocessing pipeline. Models like Mamba give you a way to process a long sequence with computation that scales linearly with its length, while selectively carrying information forward.

So the opportunity is partly efficiency, but it’s also about what that efficiency lets you model. Can you go closer to the raw signal, give the model a longer context, and let it learn the right abstractions? That’s where I think these architectures are particularly interesting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses raw data and sequence length but does not say less-optimized tokenizers improve alternative models’ performance over Transformers at matched compute.

r002.rationale: It says attention scaling is a constraint when samples carry little information, but does not explain that Transformers’ storage of past inputs is wasteful in that setting.

r003.rationale: It says Mamba selectively carries information forward, but does not clearly attribute its suitability for less-processed data to internally compressing that data.
